newsitem.title: USA: U.S. said to probe finances of second Clinton appointee.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said to probe finances of second Clinton appointee.

text.p: The Justice Department is investigating questions about the personal investments of Samuel Berger, President Bill Clinton's choice for national security adviser, the Washington Post reported on Friday.

Berger is the second member of Clinton's newly announced foreign policy team to face an inquiry about an apparent inadvertent failure to sell stocks that could represent a potential conflict of interest.
Anthony Lake, the president's choice to head the CIA, was questioned by the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section last week.

The White House said Lake had made an innocent mistake in not complying with an order to sell $200,000 worth of energy stocks and Clinton on Wednesday stood firmly behind his nominee, saying he did not believe the issue threatened Lake's Senate confirmation.
Berger, who currently is deputy national security adviser and whose promotion does not require Senate approval, faced a nearly identical set of circumstances, the Post reported.
Berger was advised in 1994 by White House lawyers that he should sell a family holding of oil stock because of a possible conflict of interest, the newspaper said.
After initially questioning the judgment, Berger agreed but then forgot to sell the stock until he was reminded by White House lawyers more than a year later.

White House chief of staff Leon Panetta and White House counsel Jack Quinn told the Post that Clinton was fully aware of the investigations into Lake and Berger at the time he announced their appointments.
The president, they said, believed that both men had committted unintentional and harmless oversights, neither of which was serious enough to stand in the way of naming them to new jobs.
